common_mistakes: Assuming the whole project needs a rewrite to scale -- actually only the transport layer (VpnNode) is scoped narrowly, not the protocol core
Conflating Peer's multi-peer capability with VpnNode's single-peer scoping as if they were the same limitation
follow_up_questions: What specifically in VpnNode would need to change to support multiple simultaneous active peers?
Would Peer's internal data structures need any change to support hundreds of trusted peers?
What's the smallest change that would let this become a usable (if minimal) real VPN client?

question: What's the exact difference between VpnNode's point-to-point scoping and Peer's underlying multi-peer capability?
answer_hinglish:
Peer class apne data structures mein kahin bhi 'ek active peer' ka assumption nahi karta -- trustedByName/trustedByKeyHex multiple peers ko trust kar sakte hain, pendingHandshakes multiple concurrent attempts ko (alag peers ke saath) track kar sakta hai, aur peerSessions/sessionsByReceiverId multiple established sessions ko ek saath hold kar sakte hain. test/peer.test.ts mein hi 3+ peers (alice, bob, impostor) involve hote hain scenarios mein.

VpnNode, jo Peer ko REAL socket se jodta hai, EXPLICITLY ek single activePeerName field rakhta hai. Yeh field pehle successful handshake par set hota hai (either as initiator via connect(), ya as responder via handleMessage's HANDSHAKE_INIT branch -- dono jagah '??=' operator use hota hai, jo sirf tab assign karta hai jab pehle se undefined ho). Iska matlab: outbound app traffic (tun.send()) hamesha EK HI destination peer ko jaata hai -- jo bhi sabse pehla successful handshake tha. Agar VpnNode doosre peer ke saath bhi handshake kare, Peer level par session install ho jaayega (kyunki Peer multi-peer capable hai), par VpnNode ka outbound traffic ab bhi FIRST peer ko hi jaayega, kyunki activePeerName change nahi hota.

Yeh deliberate simplification hai (PLAN.md documented) taaki demo aur real-socket tests simple rahein -- 'tun.send() ka destination unambiguous hai'. Protocol layer ki capability zyada hai, par transport layer iska use NAHI kar raha is stage mein.
why_needed: Yeh distinction samajhna zaroori hai pehle 'VPN concentrator' jaisi follow-up discussion ke liye -- interviewer check karega ki candidate exactly samajhta hai KAHAN limitation hai (VpnNode) aur kahan nahi (Peer).
real_world_analogy: Ek phone jo technically multiple SIM cards support karta hai (Peer ki capability), par currently software mein sirf EK SIM ko 'default outgoing' ke liye configured kiya gaya hai (VpnNode ka activePeerName) -- doosra SIM incoming calls le sakta hai, par outgoing calls hamesha default SIM se jaate hain.
how_it_works: activePeerName ??= result.peerName dono handshake-success branches mein (init aur response) hota hai -- pehla successful handshake hi 'active' ban jaata hai, future handshakes activePeerName ko overwrite nahi karte.
in_this_project: src/transport.ts::VpnNode.activePeerName aur handleAppSend; src/peer.ts mein peerSessions/sessionsByReceiverId multi-peer Maps. test/peer.test.ts 3+ peers wale scenarios.
advantages: Simple, unambiguous outbound routing for the demo and real-socket tests
Protocol layer's multi-peer capability stays available for future use without needing a rewrite
disadvantages: A second successful handshake silently does NOT become the outbound target -- could be surprising if someone expected VpnNode to route to whichever peer most recently connected
common_mistakes: Assuming Peer itself is limited to one peer, when the limitation is entirely in VpnNode
Expecting activePeerName to update on every new successful handshake, when it only sets once (??=)
follow_up_questions: What would happen if a second peer successfully handshakes with this VpnNode -- is that session unusable, or just not the outbound default?
Why does activePeerName use the ??= operator instead of a plain assignment?
What would a multi-peer-aware VpnNode need to decide outbound routing by, if not a single activePeerName?

question: What would a 'VPN concentrator' (multiple simultaneous peers routed by destination) need on top of this design?
answer_hinglish:
Ek VPN concentrator ek central node hota hai jo MULTIPLE peers ke saath simultaneously connected rehta hai, aur incoming/outgoing traffic ko SAHI peer tak route karta hai based on destination (jaise 'allowed IPs' WireGuard mein). Is project ka Peer class already most of the hard crypto/protocol work kar chuka hai multi-peer ke liye -- jo add karna padega woh mainly transport aur routing layer mein hai.

Pehla change: VpnNode jaisa single activePeerName wala design replace hoga ek ROUTING TABLE se -- destination (jaise ek virtual IP range, ya kisi bhi application-level identifier) se peerName tak ka mapping. Jab app koi outbound packet bheje, concentrator ko yeh decide karna padega KAUNSE peer ko encrypt+send karna hai, destination ke basis par -- is project mein payloads opaque bytes hain, isliye real IP-based routing ke liye payload ke andar se destination address parse karna padega (jo abhi explicitly NOT in scope hai).

Doosra: concurrent handshakes ko handle karna -- Peer already pendingHandshakes multiple concurrent attempts support karta hai (different peers ke liye), par agar SAME peer se multiple simultaneous connection attempts aayein (jaise ek client jo roam kar raha hai), extra logic chahiye hoga decide karne ke liye kaunsa 'wins'.

Teesra: per-peer resource limits aur fairness -- ek concentrator sau-hazaaron peers handle kar sakta hai, isliye memory (Session objects, AntiReplayWindow bitmaps -- har ek 256 bytes default) aur CPU (handshake ECDH computations) per-peer cost ko bound karna zaroori hoga, especially DoS resistance ke against (jo already documented 'not handled' hai is project mein).
why_needed: Yeh ek classic system-design extrapolation hai -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate chhote, working system se bade, production-shape system tak ka path articulate kar sakta hai, specific gaps naam ke sath.
real_world_analogy: Ek single-lane toll booth (VpnNode, ek gaadi ek time) vs ek multi-lane highway toll plaza (concentrator) jahan ek central system decide karta hai har gaadi kaunsi lane mein jaaye based on destination, aur system ko peak-hour load bhi handle karna padta hai bina crash kiye.
how_it_works: Peer ke existing Maps (peerSessions, sessionsByReceiverId, trustedByName) already multi-peer foundation hain -- concentrator ek naya routing/dispatch layer banayega jo yeh Maps ko destination-based decisions ke sath combine karega.
in_this_project: PLAN.md ke 'Stage 2 candidates' mein explicitly 'multiple simultaneous peers routed by destination (a real VPN concentrator shape)' mention hai, not-started.
advantages: Peer's existing multi-peer data structures mean the crypto/protocol core needs no rework
Routing/dispatch concerns stay cleanly separate from authentication/encryption concerns
disadvantages: Significant new complexity: routing tables, per-peer resource limits, DoS resistance -- none of which this project's stage 1 needed to solve
common_mistakes: Assuming a concentrator is 'just run VpnNode N times' -- that ignores shared routing/dispatch and resource-limit concerns
Forgetting that opaque-byte payloads (this project's design) would need real IP parsing for destination-based routing
follow_up_questions: How would this design need to change if payloads were real IP packets instead of opaque bytes?
What per-peer resource limits would you add first, and why?
How would you prevent one misbehaving or malicious peer from exhausting resources shared by all peers?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: A concentrator trades the simplicity of point-to-point (unambiguous destination) for routing complexity -- every outbound packet now needs a destination-resolution step, and the system must decide what happens on ambiguous or unknown destinations, which this project's point-to-point design never has to consider.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without per-peer resource bounds, a single peer repeatedly initiating (or being spoofed into appearing to initiate) handshakes could exhaust the concentrator's CPU on ECDH computations for every other legitimate peer -- exactly the DoS gap this project's README already documents as not handled, but which becomes far more consequential once many peers share one process.
advanced.alternatives: An alternative to a single monolithic concentrator process is horizontal sharding -- multiple concentrator instances, each owning a subset of peers, behind a load balancer keyed by peer identity; this avoids one process being a single point of resource contention, at the cost of needing consistent peer-to-instance assignment.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x peers, the routing table and per-peer Session/AntiReplayWindow memory grow linearly, which is fine; at 100x, handshake CPU burst (many peers reconnecting at once, e.g. after a restart) becomes the first likely bottleneck, since ECDH is the most expensive operation per peer, not the symmetric transport encryption.
advanced.production_improvements: A production concentrator would add handshake rate limiting per source address, a connection-count cap per peer identity, and likely a cookie/puzzle mechanism (like real WireGuard's) before investing CPU in a full ECDH computation for an unverified handshake attempt.

question: How does this project's handshake-plus-transport structure compare to TLS or SSH as secure-channel protocols?
answer_hinglish:
Teeno protocols (yeh project, TLS, SSH) ek hi fundamental shape follow karte hain: ek HANDSHAKE phase jo authentication + key agreement karta hai, phir ek TRANSPORT phase jo symmetric AEAD encryption se bulk data carry karta hai. Yeh shape itself universal hai secure channels ke liye.

Differences: TLS authentication ke liye mostly CERTIFICATES aur SIGNATURES use karta hai (CA-signed public keys), jabki yeh project (WireGuard ki tarah) sirf PRE-SHARED, pinned static public keys use karta hai (trustPeer() se, out-of-band) -- koi certificate authority, koi signature verification chain nahi. Yeh simpler hai par 'kisi ko pehli baar trust karna' (identity bootstrap) manual rehta hai, jabki TLS ek CA chain se automated trust deta hai.

SSH bhi key-based authentication use karta hai (known_hosts jaisa pinning, exactly WireGuard jaisa) -- isliye yeh project SSH ke philosophically zyada close hai TLS se. SSH ka handshake bhi Diffie-Hellman based key exchange use karta hai, forward secrecy ke saath, modern versions mein.

Ek aur bada difference: yeh project aur WireGuard dono UDP-based, CONNECTIONLESS transport use karte hain (per-packet encryption, kisi stream state ke bina) -- TLS aur SSH dono TCP ke upar build hote hain, ek ORDERED BYTE STREAM encrypt karte hain, record-layer framing ke sath. Is project mein har packet independently self-contained hai (apna counter, apna AEAD tag) -- TLS record bhi similar hai per-record, par TCP ki ordering guarantee par depend karta hai jo yeh project (UDP hone ki wajah se) khud anti-replay window se achieve karta hai.
why_needed: Yeh ek classic 'compare and contrast' system-design question hai jo candidate ki breadth test karta hai -- is ek project ko samajhna kaafi nahi, usse larger family of protocols ke context mein rakhna bhi expect kiya jaata hai senior-level interviews mein.
real_world_analogy: Teen alag security-check systems ek hi airport mein -- ek jo government-issued ID (certificate/CA, TLS jaisa) check karta hai, ek jo pehle se registered fingerprint (pinned key, SSH/WireGuard jaisa) check karta hai -- dono ka goal same hai ('yeh waqai wahi insaan hai'), par trust establish karne ka tareeka alag hai.
how_it_works: Handshake phase mein identity + key agreement; transport phase mein per-packet/per-record AEAD. Yeh project is shape ko minimal rakhta hai -- no certificates, no record-layer renegotiation, no stream ordering guarantee beyond anti-replay.
in_this_project: src/handshake.ts (authentication + key agreement) aur src/session.ts (transport AEAD) yeh do-phase structure clearly demonstrate karte hain. meta.json ka pitch explicitly 'TLS, SSH, aur har secure-channel protocol mein dobara aate hain' likhta hai.
advantages: Pinned-key model (no CA) is simpler to implement and reason about than certificate chains
UDP + per-packet encryption avoids TCP-over-TCP style problems that a tunneled TCP protocol would hit
disadvantages: No automated trust bootstrap (unlike TLS's CA system) -- every peer relationship needs manual out-of-band key exchange
No certificate revocation equivalent -- if a static key needs to be distrusted, every peer must be told individually
common_mistakes: Assuming TLS-style CA trust would be a drop-in replacement for this project's pinned-key trust model without other changes
Conflating 'handshake' (key agreement + auth) with 'transport' (bulk encryption) as if they were the same phase
follow_up_questions: Why might a protocol choose pinned keys (WireGuard, SSH) over a CA-based certificate model (TLS)?
What would need to change in this project to support something like certificate-based trust?
How does TLS's record layer handle ordering and replay differently than this project's anti-replay window, given TLS runs over TCP?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Pinned-key trust (this project, WireGuard, SSH) trades the operational convenience of a CA (automatic trust of any cert signed by a known root) for a smaller trust surface and no dependency on a third party, at the cost of manual, linear-effort key distribution as the number of peers grows.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If a peer's static private key is compromised, this project has no revocation mechanism -- every OTHER peer that trusted it must manually call trustPeer() again with a new key once they learn of the compromise; a CA-based system could instead publish a revocation and have it propagate.
advanced.alternatives: A middle ground some real systems use is a private CA (an internal certificate authority) that still avoids depending on public CAs but gets back some of the revocation/rotation convenience -- WireGuard itself deliberately avoids this for simplicity, same choice this project makes.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10 trusted peers, manual key distribution is manageable; at 1000s, it becomes the dominant operational cost, which is exactly why the Database Design questions in this project's question set frame peer-configuration storage as the real scaling concern, not the crypto itself.
advanced.production_improvements: A production evolution might add a lightweight, project-internal key-distribution mechanism (signed peer-config bundles distributed out of band) without going as far as a full public-key-infrastructure CA, trading some of TLS's automation for WireGuard-style simplicity.

question: If you had to add NAT traversal / endpoint roaming to VpnNode, where would you make the change, and what makes it genuinely hard?
answer_hinglish:
Is project mein yeh explicitly NOT implemented hai (README's 'Known and NOT handled'). VpnNode abhi 'remotes' Map mein peerName -> {host, port} rakhta hai, aur yeh SIRF handshake ke time learn hota hai (handleMessage mein 'this.remotes.set(result.peerName, from)') -- is address ko phir kabhi update nahi kiya jaata, chahe baad mein peer ka actual source address badal jaaye (NAT re-mapping ya network switch ki wajah se).

Main change yahi karna hoga: 'this.remotes.set(...)' SIRF handshake messages ke liye nahi, TRANSPORT_DATA packets ke liye bhi call hona chahiye -- matlab jab bhi koi successfully-decrypted packet kisi NAYE address se aaye, remotes Map ko update kar do us peer ke liye. Yeh exactly WireGuard ka 'roaming' feature hai.

Jo genuinely hard hai: decrypt SUCCESS hone ke BAAD hi address update karna chahiye (kyunki decrypt se pehle hum nahi jaante ki yeh packet REALLY us peer se hai ya koi spoofed source address wala packet hai) -- yeh is project ka already-established 'receiver-chosen id, not sender address' principle ko extend karta hai: packet KAHAN SE aaya yeh identity nahi batata, DECRYPT SUCCESS batata hai. Doosra hard part: agar attacker ek valid, replayed packet KO ek DIFFERENT fake source address se bhejta hai, naive roaming-update logic VpnNode ko confuse kar sakta hai ki 'peer naye address par chala gaya' jabki asal mein yeh replay attack hai -- isliye roaming update ko anti-replay check ke SAME 'authenticated-only' gate se guzarna chahiye, replayed packets address update trigger NAHI karna chahiye.
why_needed: Yeh ek realistic feature-extension question hai jo deep protocol understanding test karta hai -- sirf 'yeh implement nahi hai' kehna kaafi nahi, candidate ko EXACTLY design karna chahiye ki kaise aur kahan change karenge, including security pitfalls.
real_world_analogy: Ek courier jo kisi recipient ko unke registered address par deliver karta hai, par agar recipient genuinely move ho jaaye (naya address se signed, verified package receive kare), courier apna record update kar sakta hai -- par sirf ek VERIFIED signature ke baad, na ki koi bhi random postcard jo naya address claim kare usse.
how_it_works: handleMessage ke TRANSPORT_DATA branch mein, successful decrypt ke baad (result.ok === true), remotes.set(entry.peerName, from) jaisa call add hota -- authenticated hone ke baad hi, replay check pass hone ke baad.
in_this_project: src/transport.ts::handleMessage ka TRANSPORT_DATA branch abhi address update NAHI karta; README.md's 'No NAT traversal or endpoint roaming' section explicitly yeh gap documents karta hai.
advantages: Roaming support real mobile/NAT networks mein VPN ko usable banata hai bina re-handshake ke
disadvantages: Address-update logic apne aap mein ek naya attack surface hai agar authentication ke saath carefully gated na ho
common_mistakes: Address ko update karna packet arrival par bina decrypt success check kiye -- yeh spoofing ke against vulnerable hota
Yeh sochna ki roaming sirf ek 'remotes.set() yahan bhi call karo' change hai -- replay ke against gating equally important hai
follow_up_questions: What would happen if an attacker replayed an old valid packet from a different source address -- could that trick the roaming logic?
Should ALL successfully decrypted packets update the remote address, or only ones newer than the highest seen counter?
How does WireGuard itself handle this exact problem?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Updating the remote address only after successful decryption (not on raw packet arrival) trades a small amount of latency (address isn't updated until the first successfully decrypted packet from the new location) for a hard guarantee that an unauthenticated attacker cannot redirect where future outbound traffic to a peer is sent.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If address updates were gated on arrival instead of on authenticated decrypt, an attacker could send a single UDP packet with a forged header from a spoofed source address, and if it happened to pass basic parsing, redirect where the VpnNode sends its NEXT outbound packets to that peer -- a man-in-the-middle-adjacent redirection attack.
advanced.alternatives: An alternative is to require the roaming update to also pass a strictly-higher counter than previously seen (not just any valid decrypt), which additionally prevents a replayed-but-authentic old packet from a stale address from reverting a legitimate roam.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At scale with many roaming peers (e.g. mobile clients switching networks frequently), the remotes Map update becomes a hot path on every decrypt; this stays O(1) per packet, so it doesn't become a bottleneck by itself, but the overall handshake-replay-DoS surface (also not handled here) would need addressing first.
advanced.production_improvements: A production implementation would likely add a short grace/debounce window before fully committing to a new address, plus logging/metrics on address changes per peer, to make roaming behavior both robust and observable.

question: How does this project add periodic session rekeying without breaking in-flight traffic, and how is the work split between Peer, Session and VpnNode?
answer_hinglish:
Stage 2 mein rekeying built hai, aur core idea 'make-before-break' hai: naya session install hota hai, par purana turant delete nahi hota. Har peer name ke liye Peer ek PeerSessionState rakhta hai -- ek `current` Session aur at most ek `retiring` entry ({receiverId, retireAt}). Ek rekey sirf ek normal handshake hai (fresh ephemeral keys, same static keys) jo same `installSession()` path se jaata hai. Agar us peer ka session pehle se hai, toh purana session `retiring` mark hota hai `retireAt = now + rekeyGraceMs` (default 10000) ke saath, aur woh `sessionsByReceiverId` mein apne PURANE receiverId se reachable rehta hai -- apni keys aur apna AntiReplayWindow ke saath.

Send side simple hai: `encryptPacket()` hamesha `current` use karta hai, toh outbound traffic usi instant switch ho jaata hai jab local side naya session install kare. Receive side ko koi 'kaunsi key try karun' logic nahi chahiye -- har packet already receiverId carry karta hai, toh old-key wala packet automatically retiring session tak route hota hai, new-key wala current tak. Grace deadline ke baad `pruneRetiredSessions()` (jo `decryptPacket` aur `checkRekey` dono khud call karte hain) retiring entry hata deta hai.

Responsibility split clean hai: Session ko rekeying ka kuch pata nahi (sirf `sentCount` expose karta hai), Peer decide karta hai kab rekey due hai (`checkRekey(now)` -- TIME via `rekeyAfterMs`, MESSAGES via `rekeyAfterMessages`, dono opt-in), aur VpnNode actually handshake bhejta hai (`VpnNode.checkRekey`, real timer ke liye `startRekeyTimer`). Sirf original initiator rekey karta hai, aur lost rekey handshake current session ko kabhi nahi todta -- `rekeyRetryMs` (default 5000) ke baad stale attempt abandon hota hai aur retry hota hai.
why_needed: Session rekeying long-running secure channels ka real production concern hai -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate 'naya handshake chala do' se aage jaake overlap/transition problem, trigger ownership, aur layering bhi explain kar sake, aur yahan woh ACTUAL built design walk through kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek building jisme lock changed jaa rahe hain, par turant purana lock disable nahi kiya jaata -- kuch din tak dono keys (purani aur nayi) kaam karti hain, taaki jo log abhi purani key leke aaye hain woh bhi andar aa sakein jab tak unhe nayi key mil jaaye.
how_it_works: Peer.installSession(): naya Session banao; agar previous.retiring hai toh uska receiverId sessionsByReceiverId se turant delete; phir peerSessions mein {current: naya, establishedAt: now, role: previous?.role ?? defaultRole, generation: +1, retiring: {receiverId: previous.current.myReceiverId, retireAt: now + rekeyGraceMs}} set karo, aur naye myReceiverId ko sessionsByReceiverId mein register karo. decryptPacket() pehle pruneRetiredSessions() chalata hai, phir receiverId se lookup -- current ho ya retiring, dono same map mein hain.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts: PeerOptions (rekeyAfterMs, rekeyAfterMessages, rekeyRetryMs, rekeyGraceMs), PeerSessionState, installSession, encryptPacket (always current), decryptPacket + pruneRetiredSessions, checkRekey + abandonStaleRekeyAttempts. src/session.ts: sentCount getter (message-count trigger ke liye). src/transport.ts: VpnNode.checkRekey, startRekeyTimer, stopRekeyTimer, close. test/rekey.test.ts: 'a packet encrypted on the OLD session right before a rekey still decrypts correctly after the new session exists' aur real-UDP 'packets sent across two rekey boundaries all arrive exactly once, with no corruption'.
advantages: Rekeying bounds how much traffic (and how much time) any single key protects, so a key compromise has a bounded blast radius
No wire-format change and no try-each-key decrypt: the existing receiverId already tells the receiver which generation a packet belongs to
Opt-in by default, so stage 1 behavior and its whole test suite stayed unchanged
disadvantages: Up to two live sessions per peer at once, plus pending-handshake bookkeeping, is real extra state to reason about
The grace window is a fixed config value (rekeyGraceMs), not adapted to the measured round-trip time
Nothing inside Peer runs on its own -- a caller must call checkRekey() periodically (VpnNode.startRekeyTimer does this), or rekeying never happens
common_mistakes: Simply overwriting the old session the moment a new handshake completes, dropping any in-flight packet encrypted under the old key
Forgetting that BOTH sender and receiver need coordinated transition logic, not just one side
follow_up_questions: How long should rekeyGraceMs be relative to rekeyRetryMs and the real round-trip time?
Why can the receiver skip any 'which key do I try' logic during the overlap window in this design?
Why does a second rapid rekey drop the older retiring session immediately instead of keeping it?
What happens to the anti-replay window state when a new session is installed?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Make-before-break (current + one retiring session) trades the simplicity of one-session-per-peer for a bounded window of dual-session state. Break-before-make (overwrite the old session the instant a new one installs -- exactly the RK10 mutation) is simpler but drops every in-flight packet at every rekey. Keeping the decision in Peer and the timer in VpnNode keeps the protocol logic testable with ManualClock and no real timers.
advanced.failure_scenarios: A lost rekey HANDSHAKE_INIT leaves the initiator on its current session; the pending attempt is abandoned after rekeyRetryMs and retried. A grace window shorter than real network delay would let an old-key packet arrive after its receiverId is pruned (UNKNOWN_SESSION). A second rekey inside the grace window drops the older retiring session at once (tested). A lost HANDSHAKE_RESPONSE is subtler: the responder has already switched its own current session, so its outbound packets target a receiverId the initiator never installed until the retry lands -- this follows from the code, it is not covered by a test.
advanced.alternatives: A key-generation byte on the wire plus try-old-then-new decrypt (not needed here because receiverIds already disambiguate); a hash ratchet that derives the next key from the current one (cheaper, but loses the fresh-ephemeral forward secrecy a full re-handshake gives); letting either side rekey independently (rejected in PLAN.md: harmless with this design but doubles churn for zero benefit).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: With many peers on one Peer, checkRekey() is a linear scan over peerSessions and pendingHandshakes on every tick -- fine at small N; at 100x you would want a deadline-ordered structure and staggered rekey times so all sessions do not do ECDH in the same second.
advanced.production_improvements: Add jitter to rekeyAfterMs so many sessions do not rekey in lockstep, a byte-count trigger like WireGuard's, metrics on how many packets actually arrive on the retiring session (to tune rekeyGraceMs empirically), and a test for the lost-HANDSHAKE_RESPONSE path.

question: What's missing from this handshake for it to survive unmodified on the open internet, and why doesn't stage 1 need to solve it?
answer_hinglish:
Do bade gaps hain, dono README/PLAN.md mein honestly documented: handshake-replay protection, aur DoS-resistance cookie -- dono real WireGuard ke handshake mein hote hain, yahan nahi.

Handshake-replay: agar koi captured HANDSHAKE_INIT message dobara (later time par) replay kiya jaaye, yeh harmless extra attempt banata hai -- responder isse normally process karega aur ek response bhejega, par asli initiator ka already-pending attempt affected nahi hota, aur koi NAYI working session is replay se nahi banti (kyunki initiator apna match response kabhi receive/process nahi karega apne pendingHandshakes mein agar woh attempt already complete ho chuka). Real WireGuard ek TIMESTAMP add karta hai message mein taaki EK replay bhi reject ho jaaye turant.

DoS-resistance cookie: har HANDSHAKE_INIT message process karne mein EK ECDH computation + AEAD decrypt lagta hai -- yeh cheap nahi hai CPU-wise agar bahut saare fake attempts bheje jaayein. Koi rate-limit ya 'proof of work before we do expensive crypto' mechanism yahan nahi hai -- ek attacker repeatedly fake HANDSHAKE_INIT bhej ke responder ka CPU burn kar sakta hai.

Yeh gaps stage 1 ke LEARNING GOAL ke liye irrelevant hain -- stage 1 ka point ECDH authentication + forward secrecy + AEAD + anti-replay-for-TRANSPORT ko concrete samajhna tha, operational hardening (DoS resistance, handshake-replay) alag concern hain jo 'yeh protocol actually internet par deploy karne layak hai' ke liye zaroori hain, par core cryptographic correctness ko nahi affect karte. Isliye PLAN.md explicitly yeh scope out karta hai, honestly, bina 'already handled hai' claim kiye.
why_needed: Honest scoping ek senior-level signal hai -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate apne khud ke kaam ki limitations ko precisely articulate kar sakta hai, bina overselling ya underselling kiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek prototype car jo highway par chalti hai theek se, par crash-test-rated bumper ya airbags nahi hain abhi -- core driving mechanism (engine, steering) kaam karta hai aur yeh demonstrate karta hai, par 'road-ready for general public' banne se pehle safety hardening add karni padegi.
how_it_works: Handshake-replay: koi timestamp check nahi hai message 1 mein. DoS cookie: koi lightweight proof-of-work ya rate-limit step nahi hai ECDH compute karne se pehle.
in_this_project: PLAN.md ka 'Decisions' section aur README.md ka 'Known and NOT handled' section dono explicitly in dono gaps ko document karte hain.
advantages: Scope ko tightly rakhne se core concepts (ECDH auth, forward secrecy, AEAD, anti-replay) deeply aur cleanly explore hue, bina unrelated hardening complexity ke
disadvantages: Is form mein deploy karna unsafe hoga open internet par -- dono gaps real exploitable weaknesses hain, demo/learning environment ke liye nahi production ke liye
common_mistakes: Yeh samajhna ki AEAD authentication hi handshake-replay se bhi bachata hai -- woh TRANSPORT replay se bachata hai, yeh ek alag (handshake-level) gap hai
Yeh sochna ki is project ki absence of DoS protection ek bug hai -- yeh ek deliberately scoped-out decision hai, documented honestly
follow_up_questions: What specifically would a handshake-replay timestamp need to prevent, that the existing transport anti-replay window does not already cover?
What's the simplest DoS-resistance mechanism you could add before doing the expensive ECDH computation?
Why doesn't a replayed HANDSHAKE_INIT produce a usable session for the attacker, even without timestamp protection?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Deliberately scoping out DoS hardening keeps the handshake code simple and focused purely on the authentication/forward-secrecy properties being taught, at the cost of the implementation being unsafe to expose directly to an untrusted network as-is.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without a DoS cookie, a flood of fake HANDSHAKE_INIT messages (even ones that will ultimately fail AUTH_FAILED or UNTRUSTED_PEER) still cost the responder a full ECDH computation and AEAD decrypt attempt each, before rejection -- an attacker doesn't need a valid key to cause CPU exhaustion.
advanced.alternatives: A lightweight alternative to WireGuard's full MAC-cookie mechanism is a simple per-source-address rate limiter in front of handshake processing, cheaper to build than a cryptographic cookie scheme but less robust against a distributed/spoofed-source attack.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At internet scale, DoS resistance becomes the FIRST thing that must be solved before any of this project's other correctness properties even matter -- a responder that can be CPU-exhausted by handshake floods is unavailable regardless of how correct its anti-replay window or AEAD usage is.
advanced.production_improvements: A production deployment would add a handshake timestamp plus a stateless cookie/MAC challenge-response (as real WireGuard does) before committing to any ECDH computation, so that an attacker without the ability to complete a round trip (e.g. a spoofed source address) cannot cause meaningful CPU cost.

question: If you needed to persist peer configuration at scale (many trusted peers and their static public keys), what schema would you use?
answer_hinglish:
Is project mein koi database hai hi nahi -- Peer.trustedByName aur trustedByKeyHex sirf in-memory Maps hain, process restart hone par sab kuch khatam ho jaata hai (trustPeer() dobara call karna padta hai). Agar yeh production mein scale karna ho (jaise sau-hazaaron trusted peers), ek relational schema reasonable hoga:

`trusted_peers` table: columns -- id (primary key), owner_peer_id (yeh config kis Peer/node ka hai, multi-tenant scenario mein), peer_name (friendly identifier, jaise 'bob'), static_public_key (32-byte binary, UNIQUE constraint -- har key sirf ek identity represent kare), trust_added_at (timestamp), trust_added_by (audit trail ke liye), status ('active'/'revoked').

Yeh in-memory Maps ka direct translation hai: trustedByName (peerName -> key) banta hai ek INDEX peer_name par; trustedByKeyHex (key -> peerName, reverse lookup for identity verification during handshake) banta hai ek UNIQUE INDEX static_public_key par. Dono lookups bahut frequent honge (har incoming handshake par trustedByKeyHex jaisa reverse lookup zaroori hai), isliye dono columns indexed hone chahiye, static_public_key UNIQUE honi chahiye kyunki ek key sirf EK identity ko map karni chahiye.

Static key binary (BYTEA/VARBINARY, 32 bytes) store karna chahiye, hex-string nahi -- storage efficient aur comparison fast, chahe application layer mein hex ya base64 convert kiya jaa sake display ke liye.
why_needed: Yeh project mein database nahi hai, par interviewer yeh dekhna chahta hai ki candidate in-memory state ko ek persistence-worthy schema mein translate kar sakta hai, keeping the SAME lookup patterns in mind jo application already use karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek company ka badge-access system -- har employee ka ek unique badge ID hota hai (static public key jaisa), aur security system ko dono directions mein fast lookup chahiye: 'is employee ka badge kya hai' AND 'yeh badge kiska hai' (jaise entry scan hone par).
how_it_works: In-memory trustedByName Map -> indexed peer_name column; trustedByKeyHex Map -> unique indexed static_public_key column. Dono ek hi row ke do alag access patterns hain.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts mein trustedByName aur trustedByKeyHex dono Maps hain -- yeh project ka explicit statement hai ki dono directions mein fast lookup chahiye, jo schema design directly inform karta hai.
code_example:
-- illustrative, not in repo
CREATE TABLE trusted_peers (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_peer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  peer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  static_public_key BYTEA NOT NULL,
  status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',
  trust_added_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (owner_peer_id, static_public_key),
  UNIQUE (owner_peer_id, peer_name)
);
advantages: Direct mapping from the existing in-memory data structures means the lookup patterns the code already relies on are naturally supported
Binary storage for the key is compact and fast to compare/index
disadvantages: A relational schema adds operational overhead (a DB dependency) this project deliberately avoids by being a pure in-memory library
common_mistakes: Storing the static public key as a hex/base64 TEXT column without a unique index, allowing duplicate identities to be accidentally trusted under different names
Forgetting the reverse lookup (key -> peer name) that the handshake's trust-check actually needs
follow_up_questions: Why does the static public key need a UNIQUE constraint, not just an index?
How would you scope this table if one process needed to manage trusted peers for multiple local identities (owner_peer_id)?
What would a 'revoke trust' operation look like against this schema, and should it delete the row or just flip status?

question: What indexes would the peer-configuration table need, and why specifically those?
answer_hinglish:
Teen access patterns hain jo is project ka in-memory code already expose karta hai, aur har ek ko apna index chahiye.

Pehla: trustPeer(peerName, key) ka lookup-by-name -- jab koi existing peer ko re-trust kiya jaata hai (naye key ke saath), purana entry peer_name se dhoondha jaata hai. Yeh (owner_peer_id, peer_name) par ek UNIQUE index chahiye -- UNIQUE isliye kyunki ek peer_name sirf EK current trusted key ko point kare per owner.

Doosra: receiveHandshakeInit() mein trustedByKeyHex.get(revealed_static_key) -- yeh SABSE HOT PATH hai, HAR incoming handshake attempt par chalta hai. Is lookup ke liye (owner_peer_id, static_public_key) par UNIQUE index chahiye -- UNIQUE bhi isliye kyunki ek static key sirf ek identity represent kare (agar do peer names same key claim karein, system confused ho jaayega kiska session install karna hai).

Teesra, jo in-memory version mein nahi hai par production mein zaroori hoga: status='active' filter par ek partial/composite index, kyunki revoked keys ko trust-check query se exclude karna hoga EVERY single handshake attempt par -- agar yeh index missing ho, har handshake lookup table ka full scan kar sakta hai jaise entries grow karti hain, jo latency-sensitive handshake path ke liye unacceptable hai.
why_needed: Yeh is project ke EXACT access patterns (peer.ts ke dono Maps) ko database indexing strategy mein translate karne ki ability test karta hai -- generic 'index everything' answer kaafi nahi hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek library catalog jisme kitabon ko author ke naam se bhi dhoonda ja sake aur ISBN number se bhi -- dono access patterns ko fast banane ke liye dono par alag index chahiye, aur agar sirf ek index ho, doosra lookup har baar poori library scan karega.
how_it_works: trustedByName aur trustedByKeyHex dono O(1) Map lookups hain in-memory mein -- database mein yeh O(1)-ish (B-tree/hash index) lookups ban jaate hain agar sahi indexes exist karein, ya O(n) full scan agar nahi.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts mein trustedByName.get()/trustedByKeyHex.get() dono O(1) Map operations hain, jo exactly batate hain kis field par database index chahiye.
advantages: The hottest lookup (reverse key-to-identity on every handshake) stays fast regardless of table size
Mirrors the exact two Maps the in-memory code already relies on, so the mental model transfers directly
disadvantages: Two unique indexes on the same table add write overhead on every trust change -- acceptable since trust changes are rare compared to handshake lookups
common_mistakes: Indexing only peer_name and forgetting the reverse static_public_key lookup, which is the one actually on the hot handshake path
Not filtering out revoked keys at the index/query level, letting a revoked key still match during handshake
follow_up_questions: Which of these two lookups happens more often in practice -- by name or by key -- and does that change your indexing priority?
How would you handle the case where a revoked key needs to remain in the table for audit purposes but never match during a live handshake?
What would happen to handshake latency if the reverse-key index were missing on a table with a million trusted peers?

question: Why should live session state (keys, send counters, anti-replay windows) NOT be persisted to a durable database, even though peer configuration should be?
answer_hinglish:
Session state -- sendKey, recvKey, sendCounter, aur AntiReplayWindow ka bitmap -- yeh sab GENUINELY EPHEMERAL hai by design, aur persist karna SECURITY ko hi weaken karta hai, convenience nahi deta.

Pehli reason: forward secrecy. Session keys ephemeral private keys se derive hoti hain (dhES, dhEE), jinka poora purpose yeh hai ki woh memory mein hi rahein aur phir discard ho jaayein. Agar session keys ko durable storage mein likh diya jaaye, toh ek future database breach UN keys ko bhi expose kar dega -- jo exactly wahi guarantee tod deta hai jo ephemeral keys deliberately deti hain. Forward secrecy ka matlab hai 'yeh data abhi ke baad kisi tarah bhi recoverable nahi hona chahiye' -- isko database mein likhna seedha us promise ko violate karta hai.

Doosri reason: counters/replay-windows ki correctness restart-sensitive hoti hai. Agar sendCounter database se reload kiya jaaye after a crash ya restart, aur database ka write EK bhi packet se piche reh gaya ho (jo distributed systems mein bahut common hai, async writes ya crash-before-flush), ek counter REUSE ho sakta hai -- jo nonce-reuse attack ka darwaza khol deta hai. Similarly AntiReplayWindow ka bitmap agar stale state se reload ho, kuch legitimate 'already seen' counters ko fresh dikha sakta hai (false ACCEPT for a replay).

Isliye correct design hai: agar process restart ho, SESSION BHI khatam honi chahiye, aur ek FRESH handshake hona chahiye -- yeh is project ke 22-messaging project ke 'presence ko store se bahar rakho' wale reasoning se directly parallel hai (meta.json mein hi reference hai): live, fast-changing, security-critical state ko durable store mein daalna 'durability' ka wrong kaam hai, kyunki yeh state ka purpose hi HONA CHAHIYE ki yeh volatile rahe.
why_needed: Yeh ek deeply important distinction hai jo bahut developers miss karte hain -- 'sab kuch persist karo reliability ke liye' ek default instinct hai, par security-critical ephemeral state ke liye yeh exactly opposite karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek disposable visitor badge jiska code SIRF us ek visit ke liye valid hota hai -- agar building management har disposable badge code ko PERMANENTLY apne records mein likhe (future use ke liye 'convenience'), woh disposable hone ka poora point khatam ho jaata hai, aur ek future records leak sabhi purani visits expose kar dega.
how_it_works: Session object (session.ts) poori tarah in-memory hai -- sendKey/recvKey private readonly fields, sendCounter aur AntiReplayWindow ka bitmap kabhi disk ya external store ko touch nahi karte.
in_this_project: src/session.ts::Session mein koi persistence call nahi hai -- saara state class fields ke andar hi hai, process lifetime tak. meta.json explicitly messaging project ka 'presence ko store se bahar' wala same principle reference karta hai.
advantages: Keeping session state in-memory-only preserves forward secrecy as a real, enforceable property, not just a design intention
No risk of counter/replay-window state becoming stale or inconsistent from a lagging or crashed database write
disadvantages: A process restart loses all active sessions -- every peer must re-handshake, which is a real availability cost if restarts are frequent
common_mistakes: Persisting session keys 'just in case' for faster recovery after a crash, without realizing this breaks forward secrecy
Assuming all state in a system should be durable by default, without distinguishing security-sensitive ephemeral state from configuration
follow_up_questions: What would a database breach actually expose if session keys WERE persisted, versus if they are not?
How does this reasoning parallel why the messaging project (22-messaging) keeps presence out of its durable store?
If you needed fast recovery after a restart, what could you persist instead of raw session state to make re-handshaking cheaper, without compromising security?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Keeping session state purely in-memory trades fast crash recovery for a hard security guarantee -- a system that needs both would need to explicitly accept re-handshake cost on restart as the price of genuine forward secrecy, rather than trying to have both via persistence.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If session keys were persisted and a database backup or replica were ever exposed (a very common real-world breach vector, often more exposed than a live production server), every session whose keys were captured at that point would be retroactively decryptable, directly undoing forward secrecy for however much traffic was recorded.
advanced.alternatives: An alternative some systems use is persisting an encrypted-at-rest session state with a KEY-ENCRYPTING-KEY held only in memory (so a database breach alone isn't enough) -- this narrows but does not eliminate the risk, and adds real complexity for a VPN tunnel where re-handshaking is cheap anyway.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At scale, needing every peer to re-handshake after a restart could cause a connection-storm (many ECDH computations at once) -- this is a real operational concern, but solving it by persisting session state would be solving a performance problem by creating a security one; better fixes are staggered reconnect and cheap handshake cost, not persistence.
advanced.production_improvements: A production system would instead persist only durable, non-sensitive recovery hints (e.g. the peer configuration needed to re-handshake quickly) and accept that live sessions do not survive a restart, exactly the same boundary this project draws between peer configuration and session state.

question: How would you store and query trust metadata (who added a peer, when, and revocation status) alongside the static keys?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi Peer.trustPeer() koi metadata track nahi karta -- sirf peerName -> key mapping replace ho jaata hai, purana completely gone (trustedByKeyHex.delete() purani key ke liye call hota hai). Production mein trust ek AUDITABLE action hona chahiye, isliye metadata alag se model karna important hai.

Main idea: trust ko ek IMMUTABLE EVENT LOG ki tarah model karo, current-state table ke ALAG. `trust_events` table: id, owner_peer_id, peer_name, static_public_key, action ('granted'/'revoked'/'rotated'), actor (kisne yeh action kiya), reason (optional text), created_at -- yeh kabhi UPDATE ya DELETE nahi hota, sirf INSERT. `trusted_peers` (current-state table, VPN-029 wala) ko is log se DERIVE kiya jaata hai (ya ek materialized view/trigger se maintain kiya jaata hai) -- 'is peer ka CURRENT trusted key kya hai' sirf is log ke LATEST 'granted'/'rotated' event se nikalta hai, jab tak koi 'revoked' event uske baad na aaya ho.

Yeh pattern (event log + derived current state) do fayde deta hai: audit trail NEVER lose hota (chahe current state badal jaaye), aur 'yeh key kab trust ki gayi thi, kiske dwara, kab revoke hui' jaise questions directly log se answer ho jaate hain bina koi separate audit table maintain kiye. Query pattern: current state ke liye trusted_peers table hit karo (fast, indexed); history/audit ke liye trust_events ko peer_name/static_public_key se filter karke time-order mein dekho.
why_needed: Audit trails trust-management systems mein almost always zaroori hote hain production mein -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate 'mutable current state' aur 'immutable history' ko alag concerns ki tarah model kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek bank account ka current balance (fast lookup, ek number) vs uski poori transaction history (immutable log, kabhi edit nahi hoti) -- balance history se DERIVE hota hai, par history khud kabhi overwrite nahi hoti.
how_it_works: Event-sourcing-style pattern: naya event insert hota hai har trust change par; current state table ko ya application code se recompute kiya jaata hai ya database trigger se maintain kiya jaata hai.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts::trustPeer abhi koi event history nahi rakhta -- 'const previous = this.trustedByName.get(peerName); if (previous) this.trustedByKeyHex.delete(previous.toString('hex'))' sirf overwrite karta hai, purani entry permanently discard hoti hai.
code_example:
-- illustrative
CREATE TABLE trust_events (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_peer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  peer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  static_public_key BYTEA,
  action TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (action IN ('granted','revoked','rotated')),
  actor TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_trust_events_peer ON trust_events (owner_peer_id, peer_name, created_at);
advantages: Full audit history is never lost, even as current trust state changes repeatedly
Clean separation between 'what is true now' (fast lookup) and 'how did we get here' (history/compliance)
disadvantages: Event log grows unboundedly over time and needs its own retention/archival policy
Deriving current state from a log (rather than just reading a mutable row) adds complexity unless maintained incrementally
common_mistakes: Mutating the trust record in place and losing any history of what the key used to be or who changed it
Trying to answer audit questions by diffing database backups instead of having a proper event log
follow_up_questions: How would you efficiently maintain the current-state table from the event log without recomputing it from scratch on every read?
What would a 'who can revoke a peer's trust' authorization model need to look like on top of this schema?
How long should trust_events be retained, and does that differ from how long trusted_peers rows should exist?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: An event log plus derived current state trades some write-time complexity (every trust change writes an event AND updates or triggers an update to current state) for a durable, queryable history that a simple mutable row can never provide after the fact.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without an event log, if a compromised static key is later discovered to have been trusted incorrectly, there is no record of WHEN it was trusted, by WHOM, or what it replaced -- making incident response and root-cause analysis much harder after the fact.
advanced.alternatives: A simpler alternative is a single mutable row with an updated_at and updated_by column (no full history) -- cheaper to build and query, but answers only 'who last changed this,' not 'show me everything that ever happened to this peer's trust record.'
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At scale with many peers and frequent trust changes (e.g. automated rotation), the event log table becomes the fastest-growing table in the system; partitioning by time and archiving old events to cold storage keeps the hot path (current-state lookups) fast regardless of log size.
advanced.production_improvements: A production system would likely also emit these trust events to an external audit/SIEM pipeline in addition to storing them in the primary database, so security review doesn't depend solely on querying the same database the application uses operationally.

question: If you needed to support key rotation for a peer's static (long-term) key, what would the schema need to track that the project's current in-memory trustPeer() does not?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi trustPeer(peerName, newKey) sirf OVERWRITE karta hai -- purani key ka trustedByKeyHex entry delete hota hai, nayi key install hoti hai, aur PURANI key ka koi record nahi bachta. Production rotation ke liye yeh kaafi nahi hai, kyunki rotation ek INSTANT switch nahi hota real world mein -- dono peers ko COORDINATE karna padta hai (Alice naya key generate kare, Bob ko batana padega naya key trust karne ke liye, aur in BEECH mein dono purani key se bhi kaam kar sake taaki koi handshake attempt fail na ho jiski timing mismatch ho).

Schema ko do extra chaalein chahiye: pehla, EK PEER ke liye MULTIPLE 'valid' keys ko SAME time par allow karna, ek `valid_from`/`valid_until` overlapping range ke saath -- `trusted_peers` table mein ek row har key-version ke liye, status column 'active'/'grace-period'/'expired' ke saath, taaki rotation ke dauran PURANI aur NAYI dono key accept ho sakein thodi der ke liye. Doosra, ek `rotation_id` ya `previous_key_id` foreign key jo explicitly link kare ki yeh naya key row kis purani key ko REPLACE kar raha hai, taaki rotation history traceable rahe.

Application logic bhi badlegi: handshake ke time reverse lookup (trustedByKeyHex jaisa) ko SIRF 'active' status wali keys tak limit nahi karna -- 'grace-period' wali bhi match karni chahiyein, taaki rotation ke beech mein koi legitimate handshake fail na ho jiski rotation abhi doosri taraf propagate nahi hui.
why_needed: Key rotation ek common, non-trivial production requirement hai jo naive 'just overwrite the key' design se fail ho jaata hai -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate coordination/timing problem ko identify kar sake, sirf schema fields nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek office jahan door locks rotate ho rahe hain -- agar sab employees ko EK SAME second mein naya key mil jaaye toh koi problem nahi, par real world mein kuch employees ko naya key thodi der baad milega. Isliye thodi der tak DONO (purana aur naya) keys kaam karte rehte hain, jab tak sab migrate na ho jaayein.
how_it_works: Current trustPeer() ek atomic swap hai -- koi overlap period support nahi karta. Production schema ko overlapping validity windows ke saath multiple simultaneously-valid keys per peer allow karna hoga.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts::trustPeer -- 'const previous = this.trustedByName.get(peerName); if (previous) this.trustedByKeyHex.delete(...)' exactly yeh immediate, non-overlapping swap karta hai. test/peer.test.ts ka 're-trusting a peer under a new key' test yeh exact atomic-overwrite behavior verify karta hai.
advantages: Overlapping validity windows avoid a hard cutover that could break legitimate in-progress rotation
disadvantages: Supporting multiple simultaneously-valid keys per peer means the reverse (key-to-identity) lookup can no longer assume exactly one active key per peer -- more complex query logic
common_mistakes: Treating rotation as an instant atomic swap (like this project's in-memory trustPeer does) without considering the coordination gap between two independent peers
Not tracking rotation lineage (previous_key_id), making it hard to reason about 'what changed and when' during an incident
follow_up_questions: How long should the grace period be where both old and new keys are valid, and what determines that?
What happens if a handshake arrives claiming the OLD key after the grace period has ended?
Should key rotation be peer-initiated, centrally scheduled, or both?

question: How would you design storage for audit logging of handshake attempts (success/failure reasons) without that log itself becoming a security liability?
answer_hinglish:
Is project mein har handshake attempt ka result typed hai (AUTH_FAILED, UNTRUSTED_PEER, MALFORMED, HANDSHAKE_IN_PROGRESS, success) -- production mein yeh sab log karna valuable hai (debugging, security monitoring, detecting attack patterns), par SOCH-SAMAJH KE design karna padega taaki log khud attack surface na ban jaaye.

Pehla principle: KABHI bhi private keys, raw ephemeral key material, ya derived session keys log mein mat likho -- sirf METADATA (source address, timestamp, claimed peer identity agar revealed hui ho, failure reason, message type) log karo. Yeh is project ke khud ke convention se consistent hai -- receive-side methods typed REASON STRINGS return karte hain (jaise 'AUTH_FAILED'), raw crypto material kabhi expose nahi karte apne results mein.

Doosra: ek audit log jo bahut granular ho (har single handshake attempt, including legitimate retries) khud ek DoS/storage-exhaustion vector ban sakta hai agar attacker bahut saare fake attempts bhej sake aur har ek EK DB write trigger kare. Isliye sampling/rate-limiting apply karo logging ke liye bhi (jaise 'per source address, max N logged failures per minute', extra attempts sirf COUNTER increment karein, naya row nahi).

Teesra: failed-handshake logs mein 'claimed identity' (jo UNTRUSTED_PEER case mein pata chalti hai -- attacker ne KAUN SI real static public key claim ki thi) EK USEFUL security signal hai (pata chal sakta hai koi specific trusted peer ki identity impersonate ki jaa rahi hai), par isko bhi PII/sensitive-metadata ki tarah treat karo, access-controlled, kyunki yeh batata hai ki attacker ko ek real peer ki PUBLIC key pata hai (jo secret nahi hai, par phir bhi operational intelligence hai).
why_needed: Security audit logging apne aap ek naya attack surface bana sakta hai agar carelessly design kiya jaaye -- interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate 'logging good hai' se aage jaake 'logging KYA include kare, kya NAHI, aur kaise DoS-resistant ho' tak soch sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek building ka security camera footage -- useful hai incident investigation ke liye, par agar woh footage access-controlled na ho, ya agar camera system khud itna detailed ho ki storage bhar jaaye ek single person ke baar-baar guzarne se, system apne purpose ko defeat kar deta hai.
how_it_works: Current project ke typed rejection reasons (AUTH_FAILED/UNTRUSTED_PEER/MALFORMED/etc) already ek clean, metadata-only signal set hain jo direct logging ke liye suitable hain, bina kisi raw crypto material expose kiye.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts ke HandshakeInitResult/HandshakeResponseResult/DecryptPacketResult types exactly yeh typed-reason pattern follow karte hain -- koi raw key material kabhi result objects mein nahi aata.
advantages: Typed, metadata-only rejection reasons are already safe-by-design to log, no extra sanitization step needed
Rate-limited/sampled audit logging avoids the log itself becoming a resource-exhaustion vector
disadvantages: Sampling/rate-limiting audit logs means some individual failed attempts won't have their own row -- acceptable for aggregate security monitoring, less so for exhaustive forensics
common_mistakes: Logging raw handshake message bytes 'just in case,' which could include sensitive material depending on what gets captured
Not rate-limiting audit writes, letting an attacker's flood of fake handshake attempts also flood the audit log storage
follow_up_questions: What's the minimum set of fields you'd log for a failed handshake that's still useful for detecting an attack pattern?
How would you detect, from these logs alone, that someone is trying to impersonate a specific trusted peer?
Who should have access to read this audit log, and why might that access itself need to be more restricted than normal operational logs?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Logging only typed metadata (not raw crypto material) trades some forensic detail for a guarantee that the audit log itself cannot leak session-breaking secrets, even if the log store is later compromised -- the same forward-secrecy-adjacent reasoning as not persisting session state.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If raw handshake bytes or derived keys were ever logged for debugging and that log were later exposed, it could retroactively compromise sessions that were otherwise protected by forward secrecy -- turning a logging convenience into a security regression.
advanced.alternatives: An alternative to per-attempt logging is purely aggregate metrics (counts of AUTH_FAILED per minute per source, no per-attempt row at all) -- cheaper and inherently safer, but loses the ability to investigate a specific incident after the fact; a hybrid (aggregate metrics plus sampled detailed logs) balances both.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At scale, an unthrottled per-attempt audit log under attack conditions (a flood of fake handshakes) could itself become the bottleneck or storage-cost driver; rate-limiting or sampling audit writes separately from the handshake-processing rate limit (VPN-028's DoS cookie discussion) keeps logging proportionate to genuine signal.
advanced.production_improvements: A production system would likely stream these events to a dedicated security-analytics pipeline (separate from the primary application database) with its own retention and access controls, so a compromise of one system doesn't automatically expose the other.

question: At 10x/100x scale (many thousands of trusted peers, possibly across many VpnNode-like processes), what changes in how you'd store and distribute peer configuration?
answer_hinglish:
Is project mein ek single Peer object apne saare trusted peers in-memory mein rakhta hai (trustedByName/trustedByKeyHex Maps) -- yeh ek single-process, single-identity model hai. 10x scale par (jaise sau-hazaar trusted peers, ek process ke liye), in-memory Maps already fine rahenge -- 32-byte keys + metadata, yahan tak ki ek lakh entries bhi kuch MB memory hi lengi, aur O(1) hash-map lookup scale ke saath degrade nahi hota.

100x scale par, real bottleneck MEMORY nahi hota, COORDINATION hota hai -- agar yeh ek SINGLE process/identity ki jagah MANY VpnNode-like processes (jaise ek concentrator ke multiple instances, ya many edge nodes) ban jaayein, sabko SAME, CONSISTENT trusted-peer configuration dikhna chahiye. Yahan database ab sirf 'ek process ki memory ka backup' nahi hai, balki SOURCE OF TRUTH ban jaata hai jisse saare instances SYNC hote hain.

Is scale par design do changes maangta hai: pehla, read-heavy caching -- har instance apna khud ka in-memory cache rakhega (exactly is project ke Maps jaisa), par periodically ya event-driven refresh karega database se (jaise ek pub/sub invalidation message jab koi trust change ho) instead of hitting the database on every handshake. Doosra, consistency model decide karna -- agar ek instance par koi peer revoke ho gaya, kitni der mein doosre instances ko yeh pata chalna CHAHIYE? Security-critical hone ki wajah se, revocation ka propagation delay bound hona chahiye (jaise 'max 10 seconds'), jabki grant/addition thoda zyada lenient ho sakta hai. Yeh exact wahi CAP-theorem-adjacent tradeoff hai jo kisi bhi distributed configuration system ko face karna padta hai.
why_needed: Yeh is project ke single-process design se distributed-system-scale thinking tak ka jump test karta hai -- senior interviews mein yeh exact transition ('ek process mein kya kaam karta hai' se 'many processes mein kya badalta hai') bahut common hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhoti dukaan apna khud ka customer trust-list rakh sakti hai apne register mein. Ek nationwide chain ko yeh SAME trust-list saare branches mein consistent chahiye -- agar koi customer EK branch mein banned ho jaaye, doosri branch ko bhi jaldi pata chalna chahiye, warna banned customer doosri branch mein shop kar sakta hai.
how_it_works: In-memory Maps (this project) -> per-instance cache + database source-of-truth + invalidation mechanism (distributed version). Read path stays fast (cache hit); write path (trust change) propagates via the database plus an invalidation signal.
in_this_project: src/peer.ts ka trustedByName/trustedByKeyHex design single-process assumption rakhta hai -- VPN-029/VPN-030/VPN-032 ke schema designs isi ka distributed, persistent evolution hain.
advantages: Per-instance caching keeps the hot handshake-lookup path just as fast as this project's in-memory Maps, even across many processes
A database-backed source of truth makes trust changes consistent and auditable across all instances
disadvantages: Cache invalidation adds real distributed-systems complexity -- staleness windows, split-brain risk during network partitions between instances and the database
common_mistakes: Hitting the database on every single handshake attempt instead of caching, which reintroduces a slow, shared bottleneck on the hottest path in the system
Treating grant and revocation propagation delay as equally acceptable -- a stale revocation is a security gap, a stale grant is just a minor inconvenience
follow_up_questions: What's an acceptable staleness window for a revoked peer's key to still be accepted by some instance, and how would you bound it?
Would you use a pull-based refresh (periodic poll) or a push-based invalidation (pub/sub) for propagating trust changes, and why?
How does this tradeoff compare to the messaging project's approach to keeping fast-changing state (like presence) out of its durable store?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Caching trust configuration per instance trades perfect real-time consistency for low, predictable handshake latency -- the alternative (always hitting a shared database) guarantees freshness but turns the database into a single point of latency and failure for every handshake across the entire fleet.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If revocation propagation is too slow, a peer whose key was just revoked (e.g. because it was compromised) could still successfully complete handshakes against instances that haven't refreshed their cache yet -- the security-critical direction of staleness that needs the tightest bound.
advanced.alternatives: An alternative to cache-plus-invalidation is a fully centralized trust-check service that every instance calls synchronously on every handshake (no local cache at all) -- simpler consistency model, but makes that central service's availability and latency a hard dependency for every single handshake fleet-wide.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 100x scale, the invalidation mechanism itself (however it fans out trust changes to every instance) becomes the component to scale carefully -- a naive broadcast-to-all-instances approach works fine at dozens of instances but needs a proper pub/sub or gossip layer at hundreds or thousands.
advanced.production_improvements: A production system would likely use a pub/sub system (e.g. a message bus) for revocation events specifically (low latency, high priority) combined with periodic full-refresh polling as a safety net against missed messages, giving both fast revocation propagation and eventual consistency even if an invalidation message is lost.
